items.stem: Which of the following best describes "average velocity"?
options: The velocity u at the start of the time interval considered
The rate of change of displacement at a particular instant, the gradient of the displacement–time graph at that time
The total displacement divided by the total time taken
The rate of change of distance travelled, a scalar quantity
items.answer: The total displacement divided by the total time taken
items.markingKey: C. "average velocity" is the total displacement divided by the total time taken.

items.stem: Distinguish between instantaneous velocity and average velocity.
items.answer: Average velocity is total displacement over total time for an interval; instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one moment, the gradient of the s–t graph at that point.
items.markingKey: Average velocity is total displacement over total time for an interval; instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one moment, the gradient of the s–t graph at that point. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Arjun writes: "If the velocity of an object is zero, its acceleration must be zero." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A ball thrown upwards has zero velocity at the top but its acceleration is still g downwards; velocity and acceleration are independent.
items.markingKey: A ball thrown upwards has zero velocity at the top but its acceleration is still g downwards; velocity and acceleration are independent. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A tennis ball hits a wall at 15 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 8 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.080 s. Calculate the magnitude of the average acceleration during the contact.
items.answer: 288 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: D. Δv = 8 − (−15) = 23 m s⁻¹ (M1, direction change); a = Δv/Δt = 288 m s⁻² (A1).

items.stem: An orienteer in Hanoi runs 600 m east and then 200 m north. Calculate the angle of her displacement measured north of east.
items.markingKey: C. tan θ = 200/600 (M1); θ = 18.4° north of east (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "GPS speed readings are always more reliable than measuring speed with a stopwatch and tape measure."
items.answer: GPS is excellent for long journeys, but for short, precise lab measurements light gates or video analysis are more reliable; reliability depends on the scale of the measurement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: GPS avoids human reaction-time errors; it updates continuously and gives instantaneous values. Arguments against: GPS position has uncertainties of several metres, which matter over short distances; signal loss in tunnels or between buildings gives gaps; light gates and data loggers give better precision in a lab. Supported judgement: GPS is excellent for long journeys, but for short, precise lab measurements light gates or video analysis are more reliable; reliability depends on the scale of the measurement.

items.stem: Define the term "instantaneous velocity".
items.answer: The rate of change of displacement at a particular instant, the gradient of the displacement–time graph at that time
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the rate of change of displacement at a particular instant, the gradient of the displacement–time graph at that time. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: The magnitude of the average velocity over an interval is
options: less than or equal to the average speed
always equal to the average speed
always greater than the average speed
items.answer: less than or equal to the average speed
items.markingKey: A. Displacement magnitude ≤ distance.

items.stem: Explain why an object can have a speed but zero average velocity over a journey.
items.answer: Average velocity is total displacement / time; if the object returns to its starting point the displacement is zero, although distance and hence average speed are not zero.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Average velocity is total displacement / time; if the object returns to its starting point the displacement is zero, although distance and hence average speed are not zero. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about displacement, velocity and acceleration as vector quantities; instantaneous and average values is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Sofia.)
options: Speed and velocity are the same quantity with different names.
No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion).
Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and land at the same time (ignoring drag).
Acceleration depends on how quickly the velocity changes, not on its size; a car cruising at 30 m s⁻¹ has zero acceleration.
items.answer: Speed and velocity are the same quantity with different names.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only); velocity is a vector with direction, so two objects with the same speed can have different velocities.

items.stem: Noah drives 60 km on a motorway near Melbourne at 100 km h⁻¹ and then 10 km through town at 40 km h⁻¹. Calculate the average speed for the journey.
items.answer: 82.4 km h⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. Total time = 60/100 + 10/40 = 0.850 h (M1); average speed = 70/0.850 = 82.4 km h⁻¹ (A1). Not the mean of the two speeds.

items.stem: Noah walks 600 m east at 1.7 m s⁻¹ and then 900 m north at 1.7 m s⁻¹ through a park in Bogotá. Determine the magnitude of the average velocity for the whole walk.
items.markingKey: Displacement = √(600² + 900²) = 1080 m (M1); time = 600/1.7 + 900/1.7 = 882 s (M1); average velocity = 1.23 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A ferry crosses a river 240 m wide, heading straight across at 3.0 m s⁻¹ relative to the water. The river flows at 1.2 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the time to cross. (b) Determine the resultant velocity of the ferry relative to the bank. (c) Calculate how far downstream it lands. (d) State the heading needed to land directly opposite.
items.answer: (a) t = 240/3.0 = 80 s; (b) √(3.0² + 1.2²) = 3.23 m s⁻¹ at 21.8° to the line straight across; (c) 1.2 × 80 = 96 m; (d) aim upstream at sin⁻¹(1.2/3.0) = 23.6° to the straight-across line.
items.markingKey: (a) t = 240/3.0 = 80 s; (b) √(3.0² + 1.2²) = 3.23 m s⁻¹ at 21.8° to the line straight across; (c) 1.2 × 80 = 96 m; (d) aim upstream at sin⁻¹(1.2/3.0) = 23.6° to the straight-across line.

items.stem: What is the velocity of a ball thrown upwards at the highest point of its flight?
items.answer: Zero
items.markingKey: Zero (A1). It momentarily stops before falling.

items.stem: Outline how the data from an experiment testing s = ½at² for an object released from rest should be linearised, and state the features of the graph that would confirm the relationship.
items.answer: Plot s (y-axis) against t² (x-axis); gradient = ½a. The line should pass through the origin.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: s against t² (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = ½a (A1). The line should pass through the origin.

items.stem: Two cars brake with equal deceleration. Car X is moving twice as fast as car Y. The ratio of braking distances X : Y is
items.markingKey: C. s ∝ u².

items.stem: Rafael, a sprinter, accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.5 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. Calculate the distance covered in this time.
items.markingKey: C. s = ut + ½at² with u = 0 (M1); s = ½ × 2.5 × 5.0² = 31.2 m (A1).

items.stem: A safety poster in Toronto assumes a reaction time of 0.7 s and a braking deceleration of 7.1 m s⁻². Determine the stopping distance it should quote for a car moving at 50 km h⁻¹.
items.markingKey: B. v = 50/3.6 = 13.9 m s⁻¹ (M1); thinking distance = 9.73 m (A1); braking distance = v²/(2a) = 13.6 m (A1); total = 23.3 m.

items.stem: An electric bus starts from rest, accelerates at 2.0 m s⁻² for 12 s, then cruises at the speed reached for a further 30 s. Determine how far it has gone.
items.markingKey: D. Speed reached v = at = 24.0 m s⁻¹ (M1); s₁ = ½at² = 144 m (A1); s₂ = vt = 720 m; total = 864 m (A1).

items.stem: A car travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ approaches traffic lights. The driver has a reaction time of 0.70 s and the brakes give a deceleration of 6.5 m s⁻². (a) Calculate the thinking distance. (b) Calculate the braking distance. (c) The lights are 70 m away when the driver sees them change. Determine whether the car stops in time. (d) Discuss two factors that would change your answer.
items.answer: (a) 17.5 m; (b) 25²/(2 × 6.5) = 48.1 m; (c) total 65.6 m < 70 m, so it stops with 4.4 m to spare; (d) wet road reduces deceleration; tiredness or phone use increases reaction time; worn tyres/brakes.
items.markingKey: (a) 17.5 m; (b) 25²/(2 × 6.5) = 48.1 m; (c) total 65.6 m < 70 m, so it stops with 4.4 m to spare; (d) wet road reduces deceleration; tiredness or phone use increases reaction time; worn tyres/brakes.

items.stem: "Lowering speed limits in cities from 50 km h⁻¹ to 30 km h⁻¹ is justified by physics alone." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: braking distance ∝ v², so stopping distance falls by more than half; kinetic energy at impact ∝ v², reducing injury. Arguments against: journey times increase; economic and social factors (traffic flow, compliance) also matter; emissions can rise at low gears. Supported judgement: Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The velocity u at the start of the time interval considered"?
items.answer: initial velocity
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of initial velocity.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "reaction time".
items.answer: The time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a heavy and a light ball dropped together from the same height land at the same time when air resistance is negligible.
items.answer: Both experience the same gravitational acceleration g, independent of mass (the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass), so their motions are identical.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both experience the same gravitational acceleration g, independent of mass (the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass), so their motions are identical. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between thinking distance and braking distance.
items.answer: Thinking distance is covered at constant speed during the reaction time (∝ v); braking distance is covered while decelerating to rest (∝ v² for a constant braking force).
items.markingKey: Thinking distance is covered at constant speed during the reaction time (∝ v); braking distance is covered while decelerating to rest (∝ v² for a constant braking force). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A ball is thrown vertically downwards at 12.0 m s⁻¹ from the roof of a building 20 m high. Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance.
A metro train in Dubai accelerates from rest at 1.2 m s⁻² for 10 s and then travels at constant speed for 20 s. Calculate the total distance travelled.
items.markingKey: Speed reached v = at = 12.0 m s⁻¹ (M1); s₁ = ½at² = 60.0 m (A1); s₂ = vt = 240 m; total = 300 m (A1).

items.stem: Tomás drives at 50 km h⁻¹ on a dry road in Nairobi. Her reaction time is 1.0 s and the car can decelerate at 5.6 m s⁻². Calculate the total stopping distance.
items.markingKey: v = 50/3.6 = 13.9 m s⁻¹ (M1); thinking distance = 13.9 m (A1); braking distance = v²/(2a) = 17.3 m (A1); total = 31.2 m.

items.stem:
This question is about equations of motion for uniform acceleration (suvat).

(a) An electric bus starts from rest, accelerates at 2.0 m s⁻² for 15 s, then cruises at the speed reached for a further 30 s. Determine how far it has gone. [3]

(b) Explain why a heavy and a light ball dropped together from the same height land at the same time when air resistance is negligible. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Lowering speed limits in cities from 50 km h⁻¹ to 30 km h⁻¹ is justified by physics alone." [4]
items.answer: (a) 1120 m (b) Both experience the same gravitational acceleration g, independent of mass (the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass), so their motions are identical. (c) Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Speed reached v = at = 30.0 m s⁻¹ (M1); s₁ = ½at² = 225 m (A1); s₂ = vt = 900 m; total = 1120 m (A1). (b) [3 marks] Both experience the same gravitational acceleration g, independent of mass (the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass), so their motions are identical. (c) [4 marks] For: braking distance ∝ v², so stopping distance falls by more than half; kinetic energy at impact ∝ v², reducing injury. Against: journey times increase; economic and social factors (traffic flow, compliance) also matter; emissions can rise at low gears. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors.

items.stem:
A trolley is released from rest on an inclined ramp. The time t to travel a distance s down the ramp is measured with a light gate and a timer. Theory: s = ½at².

s / m | t / s
0.20 | 0.87
0.40 | 1.21
0.60 | 1.50
0.80 | 1.71
1.00 | 1.93
1.20 | 2.11

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the acceleration a of the trolley. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State a with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) t² (y) against s (x); (b) gradient ≈ 3.70 s² m⁻¹; (c) 0.540 m s⁻²; (d) (0.54 ± 0.02) m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) t² (y) against s (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 3.70 s² m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) a = 2/gradient = 0.540 m s⁻² (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.02 m s⁻²; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: What does the area under an acceleration–time graph represent?
items.answer: Change in velocity
items.markingKey: Change in velocity (A1). Δv = ∫a dt.

items.stem: Distinguish between a displacement–time graph and a distance–time graph.
items.answer: Displacement–time graphs can go down (returning towards start, negative velocity); distance–time graphs never decrease since distance is a scalar that always accumulates.
items.markingKey: Displacement–time graphs can go down (returning towards start, negative velocity); distance–time graphs never decrease since distance is a scalar that always accumulates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the instantaneous velocity can be found from a curved displacement–time graph.
items.answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at the required time; the gradient of the tangent (Δs/Δt) is the instantaneous velocity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Draw a tangent to the curve at the required time; the gradient of the tangent (Δs/Δt) is the instantaneous velocity. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An acceleration–time graph for a lift shows a constant acceleration of 3.0 m s⁻² for 6 s. The initial velocity is 0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the final velocity.
items.markingKey: Area under a–t graph = Δv = 3.0 × 6 = 18.0 m s⁻¹ (M1); v = 0 + 18.0 = 18.0 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: The displacement of a toy car is given by s = 1.3t² (s in m, t in s). Tariq draws a tangent to the s–t graph at t = 5.0 s. Calculate the gradient of the tangent.
items.markingKey: v = ds/dt = 2 × 1.3 × 5.0 (M1) = 13.0 m s⁻¹ (A1); the average velocity 6.50 m s⁻¹ is not the instantaneous value.

items.stem: A lift starts from rest, accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 2.0 s, moves at constant speed for 8.0 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3.0 s. (a) Sketch the velocity–time graph. (b) Calculate the total height risen. (c) Sketch the acceleration–time graph. (d) Calculate the average speed.
items.answer: (a) trapezium: 0 → 3.0 m s⁻¹ in 2 s, flat for 8 s, down to 0 in 3 s; (b) 3.0 + 24 + 4.5 = 31.5 m; (c) +1.5 m s⁻² for 2 s, 0 for 8 s, −1.0 m s⁻² for 3 s; (d) 31.5/13 = 2.42 m s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) trapezium: 0 → 3.0 m s⁻¹ in 2 s, flat for 8 s, down to 0 in 3 s; (b) 3.0 + 24 + 4.5 = 31.5 m; (c) +1.5 m s⁻² for 2 s, 0 for 8 s, −1.0 m s⁻² for 3 s; (d) 31.5/13 = 2.42 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gradient of a velocity–time graph"?
options: The total time a projectile spends in the air
An object that, once launched, moves under the influence of gravity (and possibly fluid resistance) only
The rate of change of displacement at a particular instant, the gradient of the displacement–time graph at that time
items.answer: The acceleration of the object
items.markingKey: C. "gradient of a velocity–time graph" is the acceleration of the object.

items.stem: Ingrid writes four statements while revising motion graphs: gradients and areas of displacement-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs. Which one is a misconception?
options: Only the vertical component is zero; the horizontal component u cos θ remains.
No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion).
The point where two lines cross on a velocity–time graph is where the two objects meet.
A ball thrown upwards has zero velocity at the top but its acceleration is still g downwards; velocity and acceleration are independent.
items.answer: The point where two lines cross on a velocity–time graph is where the two objects meet.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: It is where they have the same velocity; they meet where their displacements (areas) are equal, which needs a displacement–time graph or area comparison.

items.stem: "A horizontal line on a displacement–time graph means constant velocity." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It means zero velocity: the position is not changing, so the object is at rest.
items.markingKey: It means zero velocity: the position is not changing, so the object is at rest. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A cyclist in Oslo reaches 4 m s⁻¹ from rest in 5 s and later stops from 4 m s⁻¹ in 3 s, both uniformly. Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration while stopping.
items.markingKey: B. Deceleration = gradient of the v–t graph = 4/3 (M1) = 1.33 m s⁻² (A1).

items.stem: The displacement of a toy car is given by s = 0.41t² (s in m, t in s). Arjun draws a tangent to the s–t graph at t = 4.0 s. Calculate the gradient of the tangent.
items.markingKey: A. v = ds/dt = 2 × 0.41 × 4.0 (M1) = 3.28 m s⁻¹ (A1); the average velocity 1.64 m s⁻¹ is not the instantaneous value.

items.stem: An acceleration–time graph for a cyclist shows a constant acceleration of 2.5 m s⁻² for 5 s. The initial velocity is 0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the final velocity.
items.markingKey: B. Area under a–t graph = Δv = 2.5 × 5 = 12.5 m s⁻¹ (M1); v = 0 + 12.5 = 12.5 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about motion graphs: gradients and areas of displacement-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs.

(a) A data logger shows that a falling cone obeys s = 1.2t² for the first few seconds. Determine its instantaneous velocity at t = 2.0 s. [2]

(b) Explain how the instantaneous velocity can be found from a curved displacement–time graph. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Video analysis software gives more accurate motion graphs than data loggers with motion sensors." [4]
items.answer: (a) 4.80 m s⁻¹ (b) Draw a tangent to the curve at the required time; the gradient of the tangent (Δs/Δt) is the instantaneous velocity. (c) Each has strengths: video is better for 2D and complex motion, motion sensors for fast, precise 1D data; accuracy depends on frame rate, calibration and set-up.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] v = ds/dt = 2 × 1.2 × 2.0 (M1) = 4.80 m s⁻¹ (A1); the average velocity 2.40 m s⁻¹ is not the instantaneous value. (b) [3 marks] Draw a tangent to the curve at the required time; the gradient of the tangent (Δs/Δt) is the instantaneous velocity. (c) [4 marks] For: video can track 2D motion and many points at once; frame-by-frame analysis is cheap and widely available. Against: frame rate limits time resolution (e.g. 30 fps); parallax and scaling errors affect distance; motion sensors sample faster and give direct readings. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Each has strengths: video is better for 2D and complex motion, motion sensors for fast, precise 1D data; accuracy depends on frame rate, calibration and set-up.

items.stem: Define the term "time of flight".
items.answer: The total time a projectile spends in the air
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the total time a projectile spends in the air. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the descending part of a projectile path with drag is steeper than the ascending part.
items.answer: Drag continuously reduces the horizontal velocity, so later in the flight the horizontal component is smaller relative to the vertical one, making the path steeper.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Drag continuously reduces the horizontal velocity, so later in the flight the horizontal component is smaller relative to the vertical one, making the path steeper. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: When air resistance acts on a projectile, compared with no air resistance, the maximum height is
items.answer: lower and reached sooner
items.markingKey: A. Drag adds to gravity on the way up.

items.stem: A diver in Cape Town runs horizontally off a cliff 20 m above the water at 15 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed at which she enters the water.
A water jet from a fountain is projected at 12.0 m s⁻¹ at 50° above the horizontal from level ground. Calculate the time of flight, ignoring air resistance.
A diver in Singapore runs horizontally off a cliff 2.5 m above the water at 12 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed at which she enters the water.

A shot putter releases the shot at 15.0 m s⁻¹ at 38° above the horizontal from a height of 2.1 m. Ignore air resistance. (a) Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity. (b) Determine the time of flight. (c) Calculate the horizontal distance thrown. (d) Explain why the optimum release angle for the shot put is less than 45°.
items.answer: (a) 11.8 m s⁻¹, 9.23 m s⁻¹; (b) 2.09 s; (c) 24.7 m; (d) the release point is above the landing point, so a lower angle (and the athlete’s ability to throw faster at low angles) maximises range.
items.markingKey: (a) components (A1). (b) −2.1 = u_y t − ½gt² (M1), t = 2.09 s (A1). (c) x = 24.7 m (A1). (d) release height above ground lowers optimum angle (R1).

items.stem:
This question is about projectile motion with and without fluid resistance.

(a) A diver in Vienna runs horizontally off a cliff 2.5 m above the water at 12 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed at which she enters the water. [3]

(b) Explain the difference between the motion of a projectile with negligible air resistance and the motion of a projectile with significant air resistance. [4]

(c) "A 45° launch always gives the greatest range in sport." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of projectile motion with and without fluid resistance. [4]
items.answer: (a) 13.9 m s⁻¹ (b) Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent. (c) The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] v_y = √(2gh) = 7.00 m s⁻¹ (M1); v = √(u² + v_y²) (M1) = 13.9 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent. (c) [4 marks] For: true for level ground with negligible drag. Against: shot putters release from about 2 m above ground, so the optimum is lower; drag and lift on balls change the optimum; athletes can generate more speed at lower angles. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The total time a projectile spends in the air"?
items.answer: time of flight
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of time of flight.

items.stem: Alessia writes four statements while revising projectile motion with and without fluid resistance. Which one is a misconception?
options: Acceleration depends on how quickly the velocity changes, not on its size; a car cruising at 30 m s⁻¹ has zero acceleration.
In a vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g; differences in everyday falls come from air resistance.
A projectile keeps moving forward because a forward force acts on it.
Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and land at the same time (ignoring drag).
items.answer: A projectile keeps moving forward because a forward force acts on it.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion).

items.stem: A student claims: "A projectile keeps moving forward because a forward force acts on it." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion).
items.markingKey: No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the motion of a projectile with negligible air resistance and the motion of a projectile with significant air resistance.
items.answer: Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent.
items.markingKey: Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A javelin is projected at 15.0 m s⁻¹ at 35° above the horizontal from level ground. Calculate the time of flight, ignoring air resistance.

A ball rolls off a horizontal track at a fixed speed u and falls through a height h onto the floor. The horizontal distance x travelled is measured for different h. Theory: x = u√(2h/g).

h / m | x / m
0.20 | 0.356
0.40 | 0.507
0.60 | 0.624
0.80 | 0.717
1.00 | 0.792
1.20 | 0.876

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the launch speed u. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State u with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) x (y) against √h (x); (b) gradient ≈ 0.796 m^½; (c) 1.76 m s⁻¹; (d) (1.76 ± 0.05) m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) x (y) against √h (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.796 m^½ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) u = gradient × √(g/2) = 1.76 m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 0.05 m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A javelin is projected at 18.0 m s⁻¹ at 50° above the horizontal from level ground. Calculate the time of flight, ignoring air resistance.
"A 45° launch always gives the greatest range in sport." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: true for level ground with negligible drag. Arguments against: shot putters release from about 2 m above ground, so the optimum is lower; drag and lift on balls change the optimum; athletes can generate more speed at lower angles. Supported judgement: The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A footballer kicks a ball from the ground at 22 m s⁻¹ at 35° to the horizontal towards a goal 30 m away whose crossbar is 2.44 m high. Ignore air resistance. (a) Calculate the time for the ball to travel 30 m horizontally. (b) Determine the height of the ball at the goal line. (c) State whether it goes over the bar. (d) Explain how air resistance would change the outcome.
items.answer: (a) uₓ = 18.0 m s⁻¹, t = 1.66 s; (b) u_y = 12.6 m s⁻¹, y = 12.6 × 1.66 − 4.905 × 1.66² = 7.47 m; (c) yes, well over the bar; (d) drag reduces both components so the ball takes longer to reach 30 m and is lower, possibly under the bar.
items.markingKey: (a) uₓ = 18.0 m s⁻¹, t = 1.66 s; (b) u_y = 12.6 m s⁻¹, y = 12.6 × 1.66 − 4.905 × 1.66² = 7.47 m; (c) yes, well over the bar; (d) drag reduces both components so the ball takes longer to reach 30 m and is lower, possibly under the bar.

items.stem: A car doubles its speed. By what factor does its braking distance change for the same braking force?
items.markingKey: C. s = v²/(2a) ∝ v².

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "range"?
options: The horizontal displacement of a projectile when it returns to its launch height or reaches the ground
The rate of change of velocity, a vector quantity
The time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed
items.answer: The horizontal displacement of a projectile when it returns to its launch height or reaches the ground
items.markingKey: A. "range" is the horizontal displacement of a projectile when it returns to its launch height or reaches the ground.

items.stem: Which of the following can be negative?
items.answer: Velocity
items.markingKey: A. Velocity is a vector; its sign shows direction along a line.

items.stem: A ball is dropped and bounces several times. Taking downwards as positive, the velocity–time graph between bounces consists of
items.answer: parallel straight lines of gradient +g
items.markingKey: A. Between bounces only gravity acts.

items.stem: Nia writes: "Heavier objects fall faster in a vacuum." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In a vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g; differences in everyday falls come from air resistance.
items.markingKey: In a vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g; differences in everyday falls come from air resistance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two balls are launched from the same point with the same speed at 30° and 60° on level ground (no drag). Which statement is correct?
options: They have the same time of flight
They have the same range but the 60° ball stays in the air longer
items.answer: They have the same range but the 60° ball stays in the air longer
items.markingKey: D. R ∝ sin 2θ; time ∝ sin θ.

items.stem: Distinguish between distance and displacement.
items.answer: Distance is the scalar length of the path travelled; displacement is the vector change in position from start to finish, which can be smaller than the distance or zero.
items.markingKey: Distance is the scalar length of the path travelled; displacement is the vector change in position from start to finish, which can be smaller than the distance or zero. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain what the shape of the velocity–time graph of a skydiver shows before the parachute opens.
items.answer: The gradient (acceleration) starts at g and decreases as air resistance grows with speed; the curve levels off at terminal velocity where the resultant force is zero.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The gradient (acceleration) starts at g and decreases as air resistance grows with speed; the curve levels off at terminal velocity where the resultant force is zero. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mei writes four statements while revising equations of motion for uniform acceleration (suvat). Which one is a misconception?
options: A ball thrown upwards has zero acceleration at its highest point.
Only the vertical component is zero; the horizontal component u cos θ remains.
No forward force is needed; it continues by inertia (Newton’s first law). The only force is gravity (plus drag, which opposes motion).
A ball thrown upwards has zero velocity at the top but its acceleration is still g downwards; velocity and acceleration are independent.
items.answer: A ball thrown upwards has zero acceleration at its highest point.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Its velocity is zero there, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout the flight.

items.stem: A parcel is released from a drone flying horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹ at a height of 5.0 m. Calculate the time it takes to reach the ground, ignoring air resistance.
items.markingKey: C. Vertical: h = ½gt² (horizontal speed irrelevant) (M1); t = 1.01 s (A1).

items.stem: Ingrid timed a dynamics trolley between two light gates. The 5 readings of the time for a trolley to pass between two light gates 0.500 m apart were 0.667, 0.669, 0.668, 0.654, 0.628 s. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 0.657 s (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.021 s (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.021/0.657 × 100 = 3.1 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: The displacement of a toy car is given by s = 0.48t² (s in m, t in s). Sofia draws a tangent to the s–t graph at t = 2.0 s. Calculate the gradient of the tangent.
items.markingKey: A. v = ds/dt = 2 × 0.48 × 2.0 (M1) = 1.92 m s⁻¹ (A1); the average velocity 0.960 m s⁻¹ is not the instantaneous value.

items.stem: "Heavier objects fall faster in a vacuum." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In a vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g; differences in everyday falls come from air resistance.
items.markingKey: In a vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g; differences in everyday falls come from air resistance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "A bullet fired horizontally hits the ground later than one dropped from the same height at the same instant." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and land at the same time (ignoring drag).
items.markingKey: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start with zero vertical velocity and land at the same time (ignoring drag). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A cyclist travelling north at 8 m s⁻¹ turns and is travelling east at 10 m s⁻¹ 0.5 s later. Calculate the magnitude of the average acceleration.
items.markingKey: Δv = √(8² + 10²) = 12.8 m s⁻¹ (vector subtraction) (M1); a = 25.6 m s⁻² (A1).

items.stem: A data logger shows that a falling cone obeys s = 0.79t² for the first few seconds. Determine its instantaneous velocity at t = 2.0 s.
items.markingKey: v = ds/dt = 2 × 0.79 × 2.0 (M1) = 3.16 m s⁻¹ (A1); the average velocity 1.58 m s⁻¹ is not the instantaneous value.

items.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 24.0 m s⁻¹ from the edge of a cliff 25 m above the sea. Ignore air resistance. (a) Calculate the maximum height above the sea. (b) Determine the total time until it hits the sea. (c) Sketch the velocity–time graph for the motion, taking upwards as positive, and state its gradient.
items.answer: (a) 54.4 m; (b) 5.78 s; (c) straight line from +24.0 m s⁻¹ crossing zero at 2.45 s, gradient −9.81 m s⁻².
items.markingKey: (a) h = 25 + u²/2g (M1) = 54.4 m (A1). (b) −25 = 24.0t − 4.905t² (M1); t = 5.78 s (A1). (c) straight line, negative constant gradient −g (A1).

items.stem:
This question is about projectile motion with and without fluid resistance.

(a) A water jet from a fountain is launched from ground level at 18.0 m s⁻¹ at 60° to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, calculate the maximum height reached. [3]

(b) Distinguish between the motion of a projectile with negligible air resistance and the motion of a projectile with significant air resistance. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "A 45° launch always gives the greatest range in sport." [4]
items.answer: (a) 12.4 m (b) Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent. (c) The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] u_y = 18.0 sin 60° = 15.6 m s⁻¹ (M1); H = u_y²/(2g) (M1) = 12.4 m (A1). (b) [4 marks] Without drag the horizontal velocity is constant and the path is a symmetric parabola; with drag both components are reduced, the range and height fall and the descent is steeper than the ascent. (c) [4 marks] For: true for level ground with negligible drag. Against: shot putters release from about 2 m above ground, so the optimum is lower; drag and lift on balls change the optimum; athletes can generate more speed at lower angles. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The 45° result is an idealisation; real optimum angles depend on release height, drag and biomechanics, usually 35°–42°.

items.stem:
This question is about displacement, velocity and acceleration as vector quantities; instantaneous and average values.

(a) An orienteer in Cape Town runs 400 m east and then 900 m north. Calculate the angle of her displacement measured north of east. [2]

(b) Explain why an object can have a speed but zero average velocity over a journey. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "GPS speed readings are always more reliable than measuring speed with a stopwatch and tape measure." [4]
items.answer: (a) 66.0° (b) Average velocity is total displacement / time; if the object returns to its starting point the displacement is zero, although distance and hence average speed are not zero. (c) GPS is excellent for long journeys, but for short, precise lab measurements light gates or video analysis are more reliable; reliability depends on the scale of the measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] tan θ = 900/400 (M1); θ = 66.0° north of east (A1). (b) [3 marks] Average velocity is total displacement / time; if the object returns to its starting point the displacement is zero, although distance and hence average speed are not zero. (c) [4 marks] For: GPS avoids human reaction-time errors; it updates continuously and gives instantaneous values. Against: GPS position has uncertainties of several metres, which matter over short distances; signal loss in tunnels or between buildings gives gaps; light gates and data loggers give better precision in a lab. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: GPS is excellent for long journeys, but for short, precise lab measurements light gates or video analysis are more reliable; reliability depends on the scale of the measurement.

items.stem: "Video analysis software gives more accurate motion graphs than data loggers with motion sensors." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Each has strengths: video is better for 2D and complex motion, motion sensors for fast, precise 1D data; accuracy depends on frame rate, calibration and set-up.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: video can track 2D motion and many points at once; frame-by-frame analysis is cheap and widely available. Arguments against: frame rate limits time resolution (e.g. 30 fps); parallax and scaling errors affect distance; motion sensors sample faster and give direct readings. Supported judgement: Each has strengths: video is better for 2D and complex motion, motion sensors for fast, precise 1D data; accuracy depends on frame rate, calibration and set-up. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reaction time"?
options: Acceleration that is constant in both magnitude and direction
The total time a projectile spends in the air
The rate of change of velocity, a vector quantity
The time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed
items.answer: The time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed
items.markingKey: D. "reaction time" is the time between a stimulus and the start of a response, during which a driver travels at constant speed.

items.stem: For a projectile with negligible air resistance, which quantity stays constant during the flight?
items.answer: The horizontal component of velocity
items.markingKey: B. No horizontal force acts.

items.stem: Which quantity is given by the gradient of a displacement–time graph?
items.answer: Velocity
items.markingKey: Velocity (A1). v = Δs/Δt.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about motion graphs: gradients and areas of displacement-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Priya.)
options: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only); velocity is a vector with direction, so two objects with the same speed can have different velocities.
Only the vertical component is zero; the horizontal component u cos θ remains.
A horizontal line on a displacement–time graph means constant velocity.
Acceleration depends on how quickly the velocity changes, not on its size; a car cruising at 30 m s⁻¹ has zero acceleration.
items.answer: A horizontal line on a displacement–time graph means constant velocity.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: It means zero velocity: the position is not changing, so the object is at rest.

items.stem: An object falls from rest. The distances fallen in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio
items.markingKey: D. Cumulative distances go as 1 : 4 : 9 : 16; differences are odd numbers.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile can be treated independently.
items.answer: They are perpendicular components; the only force (gravity) acts vertically, so it changes only the vertical velocity while the horizontal velocity is unaffected.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are perpendicular components; the only force (gravity) acts vertically, so it changes only the vertical velocity while the horizontal velocity is unaffected. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An object moving in the negative direction has a positive acceleration. The object is
items.answer: slowing down
items.markingKey: D. Acceleration opposite to velocity reduces the speed.

items.stem: The gradient of a tangent to a velocity–time graph gives the
items.answer: instantaneous acceleration
items.markingKey: B. a = dv/dt.

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship s = ½at² for an object released from rest is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot s (y-axis) against t² (x-axis); gradient = ½a. The line should pass through the origin.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: s against t² (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = ½a (A1). The line should pass through the origin.

items.stem: A javelin is launched from ground level at 12.0 m s⁻¹ at 35° to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, calculate the maximum height reached.
Omar drives 60 km on a motorway near Seoul at 80 km h⁻¹ and then 10 km through town at 30 km h⁻¹. Calculate the average speed for the journey.
items.answer: 64.6 km h⁻¹
items.markingKey: Total time = 60/80 + 10/30 = 1.08 h (M1); average speed = 70/1.08 = 64.6 km h⁻¹ (A1). Not the mean of the two speeds.

items.stem: "A velocity–time graph that slopes downwards shows the object moving backwards." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It shows decreasing velocity (deceleration if v > 0); the object only moves backwards when v itself is negative, below the time axis.
items.markingKey: It shows decreasing velocity (deceleration if v > 0); the object only moves backwards when v itself is negative, below the time axis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Noah drives 40 km on a motorway near Oslo at 60 km h⁻¹ and then 10 km through town at 50 km h⁻¹. Calculate the average speed for the journey.
items.answer: 57.7 km h⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. Total time = 40/60 + 10/50 = 0.867 h (M1); average speed = 50/0.867 = 57.7 km h⁻¹ (A1). Not the mean of the two speeds.

items.stem: A cyclist in Nairobi accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m s⁻¹ in 3 s, travels at this speed for 10 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. Using the area under the velocity–time graph, calculate the total distance travelled.

This question is about equations of motion for uniform acceleration (suvat).

(a) A safety poster in Vienna assumes a reaction time of 0.6 s and a braking deceleration of 7.0 m s⁻². Determine the stopping distance it should quote for a car moving at 113 km h⁻¹. [3]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why the thinking distance of a driver is proportional to speed while the braking distance is proportional to the square of the speed. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Lowering speed limits in cities from 50 km h⁻¹ to 30 km h⁻¹ is justified by physics alone." [4]
items.answer: (a) 88.8 m (b) During the reaction time the car moves at constant speed, so distance = v × t_r ∝ v; while braking at constant deceleration v² = 2as, so s = v²/(2a) ∝ v². (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] v = 113/3.6 = 31.3 m s⁻¹ (M1); thinking distance = 18.8 m (A1); braking distance = v²/(2a) = 70.0 m (A1); total = 88.8 m. (b) [3 marks] During the reaction time the car moves at constant speed, so distance = v × t_r ∝ v; while braking at constant deceleration v² = 2as, so s = v²/(2a) ∝ v². (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: braking distance ∝ v², so stopping distance falls by more than half; kinetic energy at impact ∝ v², reducing injury. Against: journey times increase; economic and social factors (traffic flow, compliance) also matter; emissions can rise at low gears. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Physics gives a strong safety case (stopping distance and impact energy fall sharply), but the decision also weighs social, economic and environmental factors.
